energy.overview: Nuclear is the dominant story: restart projects (Crane/Three Mile Island, Duane Arnold) are running ahead of schedule while SMR developers rack up federal funding, IPOs, and mega-scale utility deals (TVA-ENTRA1's prospective 6-8 GW), even as pre-revenue SMR stocks have sold off sharply this year on execution-risk concerns. Long-duration storage (Form Energy, Antora) and utility M&A (NextEra-Dominion) show capital continuing to flood toward firm, always-on power for data centers, but grid interconnection queues and first-of-a-kind cost risk remain the binding constraints on how fast any of this actually reaches AI campuses.

cooling.overview: Cooling has flipped from a supporting infrastructure line to the AI buildout's central bottleneck, evidenced by a wave of multibillion-dollar strategic consolidation (Ecolab-CoolIT, Eaton-Boyd Thermal, Trane-LiquidStack) and record public-company results at Vertiv, Schneider Electric and Modine. Single-phase direct-to-chip cooling has become the default architecture for new AI clusters while air cooling is pushed into a hybrid, supporting role, and two-phase/immersion technologies are racing to prove themselves for the next density tier above 200kW racks.

power.overview: Order books and backlogs at the major electrical-equipment OEMs are expanding at a pace few industrials have ever seen -- GE Vernova's backlog hit $176B and Siemens Energy's grid unit hit a record €51B backlog -- but physical throughput hasn't caught up, with switchgear and large power transformers still quoting multi-year lead times. That mismatch is pushing power delivery further downstream into silicon (Vicor's vertical power delivery, AmberSemi's backside PowerTile) and into software that squeezes more out of the existing grid (Emerald AI, Verrus, Amperon), rather than waiting for new copper and steel capacity. Net effect: demand-side momentum is accelerating even as the physical bottleneck keeps a lid on how fast gigawatts actually get energized.

silicon.overview: The leading-edge fab and memory layer is in the middle of a structural supercycle: TSMC is pulling further ahead on 2nm yield and share while pouring another $100B into Arizona, and HBM/DRAM capacity is sold out for years as AI accelerators eat an ever-larger share of every wafer. Samsung and Intel are showing real technical progress (Samsung's HBM4 recovery, Intel's 18A-P risk production) but remain structurally behind, while SK Hynix and Micron are converting scarcity into record profits, buybacks, and a possible Solidigm IPO. The main tension for the next few years is whether the wave of new fabs (TSMC Arizona, Micron New York, SK Hynix Indiana, Rapidus) arrives fast enough to cool prices, or whether the memory shortage genuinely persists toward 2030 as SK Hynix's own CEO now warns.

compute.overview: Compute demand keeps outrunning supply: Nvidia and Broadcom both just posted record AI quarters (Nvidia's data center revenue hit $89B, Broadcom's AI semiconductor revenue jumped 221% YoY) while Marvell's expanded Google custom-silicon warrant deal shows hyperscalers actively diversifying their ASIC supply base beyond any single vendor. The binding constraint has shifted from GPU/ASIC design itself to the memory and packaging supply chain — an HBM/DRAM shortage severe enough that Nvidia delayed its next gaming GPU generation to protect AI-chip memory allocation — even as inference-focused challengers (Groq, SambaNova) reshuffle their business models and capital structures to chase the same compute crunch.

networking.overview: Every layer of the AI networking stack is re-rating upward simultaneously: transceiver makers are raising guidance mid-quarter on 1.6T ramp demand, co-packaged optics has crossed from demo to shipping product on Broadcom and Nvidia platforms, and switch vendors are posting record quarters as Ethernet displaces InfiniBand in AI back-ends. The key structural shift is that networking capex is increasingly gating AI buildouts as much as GPU supply, pushing hyperscalers and chipmakers to lock in optics capacity years in advance via direct equity investment rather than pure purchase orders.

serversdc.overview: Server OEMs and data center operators are riding a second wave of AI capex upgrades: Dell and HPE both raised full-year guidance and saw double-digit stock pops on record AI server backlogs, while Equinix used its first-ever customer summit to push into AI inference and complete a $4B Nordic acquisition. Meanwhile the operator layer is being reshaped by a private-equity-to-public pivot, with Vantage, CyrusOne and Switch all lining up IPOs even as projects like QTS's $30B Virginia campus get killed by permitting and community pushback, showing capital availability is outrunning physical siting capacity.

cloud.overview: Hyperscaler cloud growth reaccelerated sharply in Q2 CY2026, with Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure both posting their fastest growth in years while combined Big Tech AI capex guidance pushed toward $700-800B for 2026, yet free cash flow at Amazon and Alphabet is compressing hard as spending outruns revenue recognition. Neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius rode the same wave with triple-digit revenue growth and swelling backlogs, but their debt-heavy financing models drew fresh scrutiny in mid-August when rising rates triggered a sharp, if brief, selloff. The layer's central tension is now financing structure rather than demand: backlogs are enormous and real, but converting them into cash without over-leveraging balance sheets is the swing factor for 2027-2028.

applications.overview: The application layer is compounding on two axes at once: frontier labs are shipping new flagship models almost monthly (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable/Mythos 5.1, Gemini 3.7/3.8 Flash, Grok 4.6) while enterprise incumbents (Salesforce, ServiceNow, Adobe, Microsoft) are converting agentic AI into real, fast-growing recurring revenue lines rather than pilots. At the same time, two IPO trains — OpenAI toward a reported $1T target and Anthropic toward a rumored $2T target as soon as October — are forcing public markets to price frontier-lab economics for the first time, even as reports of enterprises defecting to 'good enough' open-weight models introduce a genuine margin-compression risk.
